title: The Crucible
wiki_lead:
The Crucible is a 1953 play by the American playwright Arthur Miller. It is a dramatized and partially fictionalized story of the Salem witch trials that took place in the Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1692 to 1693. Miller wrote the play as an allegory for McCarthyism, when the United States government persecuted people accused of being communists. Miller was later questioned by the House of Representatives' Committee on Un-American Activities in 1956 and convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing to identify others present at meetings he had attended.
The play was first performed at the Martin Beck Theatre on Broadway on January 22, 1953, starring E. G. Marshall, Beatrice Straight and Madeleine Sherwood. Miller felt that this production was too stylized and cold, and the reviews for it were largely hostile (although The New York Times noted "a powerful play [in a] driving performance"). The production won the 1953 Tony Award for Best Play. A year later, a new production succeeded and the play became a classic. It is regarded as a central work in the canon of American drama.

The Crucible is a 1953 play by the American playwright Arthur Miller. It is a dramatized and partially fictionalized story of the Salem witch trials that took place in the Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1692 to 1693. Miller wrote the play as an allegory for McCarthyism, when the United States government persecuted people accused of being communists. Miller was later questioned by the House of Representatives' Committee on Un-American Activities in 1956 and convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing to identify others present at meetings he had attended.
The play was first performed at the Martin Beck Theatre on Broadway on January 22, 1953, starring E. G. Marshall, Beatrice Straight and Madeleine Sherwood. Miller felt that this production was too stylized and cold, and the reviews for it were largely hostile (although The New York Times noted "a powerful play [in a] driving performance"). The production won the 1953 Tony Award for Best Play. A year later, a new production succeeded and the play became a classic. It is regarded as a central work in the canon of American drama.


Plot


Act One
In Salem, Province of Massachusetts Bay, Puritan colonists lead an isolated theocracy in constant conflict with Native Americans. The story begins with Betty Parris lying motionless in an attic. The previous evening, her father Samuel Parris witnessed her, some other girls, and his slave Tituba dancing in the forest while naked. The village becomes rife with rumors of witchcraft. Parris is concerned that the event will cause him to be removed from his position as the town's preacher. He questions his niece and adopted daughter Abigail Williams. Abigail denies that her and the girls were engaged in witchcraft. Afterwards, Thomas Putnam and his wife Ann arrive. At the Putnams' urging, Parris reluctantly reveals that he has invited John Hale to investigate. Betty attempts to jump out of the window, and Abigail coerces the others to "stick to their story" of merely dancing in the woods. They comply out of fear of being labelled witches, despite trying to conjure a curse against Elizabeth Proctor that night. Betty then passes out. 
John Proctor, Elizabeth's husband, arrives and sends the other girls out and confronts Abigail, who denies allegations of witchcraft. It is revealed that Abigail once worked as a servant for the Proctors, and that she and John had an affair, for which she was fired. Abigail still harbors feelings for John and believes they are reciprocated, but John denies this. Abigail angrily mocks John for denying his true feelings for her. Meanwhile, Betty bolts upright and begins screaming. Parris runs back into the bedroom and various villagers arrive. Abigail, standing quietly in a corner, witnesses them bickering over witchcraft, Betty's health, and Parris' pay as minister.
John Hale arrives and questions Parris, Abigail and Tituba over the girls' activities in the woods. Abigail claims Tituba forced her to drink blood; Tituba instead states that Abigail begged her to conjure a deadly curse. Parris threatens to whip Tituba to death if she does not confess to witchcraft. Tituba breaks down and falsely claims that the Devil is bewitching her and others in town and accuses Sarah Osborne and Sarah Good of witchcraft. Mrs. Putnam identifies Osborne as her former midwife and asserts that she must have killed her children. Abigail decides to play along with Tituba in order to prevent others from discovering her affair with Proctor. She leaps up, begins contorting wildly, and names Osborne, Good, and Bridget Bishop as having been "dancing with the devil". Betty suddenly rises and begins mimicking Abigail's movements and words, and accuses George Jacobs. The three continue with their accusations as Hale orders the arrest of the named people and sends for judges to try them.


Act Two
John and Elizabeth are incredulous that nearly forty people have been arrested for witchcraft. John knows that these allegations are untrue, as Abigail told him such, but is unsure of how to confess without revealing their affair. Elizabeth is disconcerted to learn her husband was alone with Abigail, who she believes still lusts after him. Mary Warren, the Proctors' servant, arrives at the Proctors' home and gives Elizabeth a poppet that she made while serving as a court witness. She reveals that 39 of the accused have been arrested so far, and might be hanged. She also reveals that Goody Osborne will be hanged, but Sarah Good's life is safe, as she confessed that she made a compact with Lucifer to torment Christians. Angered that Mary is neglecting her duties, John threatens to beat her. Mary retorts that she is now an official in the court, and that she must appear there on a daily basis. It is revealed that Elizabeth was to be arrested until Mary spoke in her defense. Mary refuses to identify Elizabeth's accuser, but Elizabeth surmises accurately that it was Abigail. She implores John to tell the court that the witchcraft allegations are false. John is reluctant, fearing that doing so will require him to reveal his affair.
Hale arrives at the Proctors' home, stating that he is interviewing all of the accused. He mentions that Rebecca Nurse was also named, but admits that he doubts this due to her extreme piousness, though he emphasizes that anything is possible. Hale is skeptical about the Proctors' religiousness, noting that they do not attend church regularly and that one of their three sons has not been baptized; John replies that this is due to his disdain for Parris. Challenged to recite the Ten Commandments, John forgets "thou shalt not commit adultery". When Hale questions her, Elizabeth is angered that he did not question Abigail first. At Elizabeth's urging, John tells Hale he knows that the accusations are fake. When Hale responds that many of the accused have confessed, John points out that they were to be hanged if they did not; Hale reluctantly acknowledges this. Giles Corey and Francis Nurse enter the house and inform John and Hale that both of their wives have been arrested for witchcraft, on account of reading "suspicious" books and sacrificing children, respectively. 
A posse led by clerk Ezekiel Cheever and town marshal George Herrick arrive soon afterwards and present a warrant for Elizabeth's arrest, much to Hale's surprise. He informs John that Abigail had a pain-induced fit earlier that evening and a needle was found stuck in her stomach; Abigail claimed that Elizabeth stabbed her with the poppet's needle through witchcraft. Mary asserts that she made the doll and stuck the needle into it, and that Abigail saw her do so. Cheever is unconvinced and prepares to arrest Elizabeth. John angrily tears the warrant to shreds and threatens Herrick and Cheever until Elizabeth calms him down and surrenders herself. He calls Hale a coward and asks him why the accusers remain unchallenged. Hale suggests that misfortune has befallen Salem because of an unmasked crime. John then orders Mary to go to court with him and expose the other girls' lies, but she protests. Aware of John's affair, she warns him that Abigail is willing to expose it if necessary. John is shocked but determines that the truth must prevail.


Act Three
37 days later, Martha Corey is on trial in court. Francis and Giles desperately interrupt the proceedings, demanding to be heard. The men are thrown out of the main room. John Proctor arrives with Mary Warren and they inform Deputy Governor Danforth and Judge Hathorne about the girls' lies. Danforth then informs an unaware John that Elizabeth is pregnant, and promises to spare her from execution until the child is born, hoping to persuade John to withdraw his case. John refuses to back down and submits a deposition signed by 91 locals attesting to the good character of Elizabeth, Rebecca Nurse and Martha Corey; Herrick also attests to John's truthfulness as well. The deposition is dismissed by Parris and Hathorne as illegal.  Hale criticizes the decision and demands to know why the accused canot defend themselves. Danforth replies that the word of the accused cannot be trusted given the "invisible nature" of witchcraft. 
Danforth then orders that all 91 locals named in the deposition be arrested for questioning. Giles Corey submits his own deposition, accusing Thomas Putnam of forcing his daughter to accuse George Jacobs in order to buy up his land. When asked by Hathorne to reveal the source of his information, Giles refuses, fearing that they will also be arrested. When Danforth threatens him with arrest for contempt, Giles argues that he cannot be arrested for "contempt of a hearing." Danforth then declares the court in session and Giles is arrested.  John submits Mary's deposition, which declares that she was coerced to accuse people by Abigail. Abigail denies Mary's assertions that they are pretending, and stands by her story about the poppet. When told by Parris and Hathorne to "pretend to be possessed", Mary is too afraid to comply. John reveals that Abigail and the other girls were caught dancing naked in the woods by Parris on the night of Betty Parris' alleged "bewitchment". When Danforth begins to question Abigail, she claims that Mary has begun to bewitch her with a cold wind and John loses his temper. He confesses their affair, Abigail's resulting firing, and Abigail's attempts to murder Elizabeth.
Danforth brings Elizabeth in to confirm this story. Unaware of John's public confession, Elizabeth lies and states that there was no affair, and that she fired Abigail out of wild suspicion. Hale begs Danforth to reconsider his judgement, but Danforth throws out this testimony based solely upon John's earlier assertion that Elizabeth would never tell a lie. Abigail and the girls run about screaming, claiming that Mary's spirit is attacking them. When Danforth announces Mary's death sentence, she recants her allegations against them, claiming that John Proctor forced her to turn against the others and that he harbors the devil. John, having given up all hope, declares that "God is dead", and is arrested. Furious, Hale denounces the proceedings and leaves the court.


Act Four
Three months later in the town jail, Tituba, sharing a cell with Sarah Good, starts hearing voices and claims that she can talk to Satan. Herrick, depressed at having arrested so many of his neighbors, has turned to alcoholism. Many villagers have been charged with witchcraft; while most have been imprisoned due to a confession, 12 have been executed. 7 more are to be hanged at sunrise for refusing to confess including John Proctor, Rebecca Nurse and Martha Corey. Giles Corey was pressed to death as the court attempted to extract a plea; though by holding out, Giles ensured that his sons would inherit his property. The village has become dysfunctional, and news of rebellion against the courts in nearby Andover arrives. Abigail, fearful of the consequences, steals Parris's life savings and boards a ship to England with Mercy Lewis. Danforth and Hathorne have returned to Salem to meet with Parris, and are surprised to learn that Hale is meeting with the condemned. Parris, who has lost everything to Abigail, reports that he has received death threats. He begs Danforth to postpone the executions in order to secure confessions. Hale, deeply remorseful and blaming himself, has returned to ask the accused to falsely confess and avoid execution. He presses Danforth to pardon the remaining seven and put the entire affair behind them. Danforth refuses, stating that pardons or postponement would cast doubt on the veracity of previous confessions and hangings.
Danforth and Hale summon Elizabeth and ask her to persuade John to confess. She is bitter towards Hale, both for doubting her earlier and for wanting John to ruin his good name, but agrees to speak with her husband. grok_lead: The Crucible is a four-act tragedy written by American playwright Arthur Miller, first performed on Broadway on January 22, 1953. The play dramatizes the Salem witch trials of 1692â1693 in colonial Massachusetts, portraying how accusations of witchcraft ignited mass hysteria, leading to the arrests, trials, and executions of numerous individuals, including the central character, farmer John Proctor. Miller composed The Crucible amid the anti-communist investigations of the early 1950s, using the historical events of Salemâwhere spectral evidence and unsubstantiated claims drove the proceedingsâas an allegory for the tactics of Senator Joseph McCarthy and the House Un-American Activities Committee. While critiquing the paranoia and civil liberties violations of these modern "witch hunts," Miller acknowledged in reflections that fears of communist infiltration drew partial legitimacy from Soviet espionage activities and global communist advances, such as the 1949 triumph of Mao Zedong in China. The narrative centers on Proctor's moral struggle after his former servant, Abigail Williams, falsely accuses his wife Elizabeth of witchcraft in a vengeful scheme rooted in their past affair, exposing broader community fractures involving greed, vengeance, and religious zealotry. Though grounded in historical records, the play incorporates fictional elements, such as amplifying personal motivations and ages of key figures like Abigail, who was 11 during the trials rather than a teenager. Upon release, The Crucible received the 1953 Tony Award for Best Play despite initial mixed reviews amid the era's tensions, and it has since achieved enduring acclaim for probing themes of truth, integrity, and the perils of ideological conformity. Adaptations include a 1957 French film and the 1996 Hollywood version directed by Nicholas Hytner, starring Daniel Day-Lewis as Proctor, which garnered Oscar nominations for Best Screenplay and Best Supporting Actress.
